content.overview: Harvest handling should minimize contamination while protecting worker safety and material identity. Sanitation, cleanable tools/surfaces, controlled movement and defined clean/dirty transitions matter from cutting through staging.

vocabulary.definition: Controlled handling intended to reduce introduction or spread of contamination during harvest and transfer.
Movement sequence designed to reduce transfer from higher-risk material or surfaces back into cleaner operations.
Tool, table, container or equipment surface that can contact harvested material.

sections.title: Tools and contact surfaces are part of product control
sections.body: Harvest tools, totes, tables and carts should follow the approved cleaning/sanitation process and remain traceable to the work area or lot where required.

sections.title: Movement can spread contamination
sections.body: People, tools and containers moving between suspect and unaffected material can transfer biological or physical contamination. Use defined workflow and separation.

sections.title: Safety still controls
sections.body: Cutting tools, lifting, powered equipment and chemical sanitation remain subject to PPE, ergonomics and task-authority requirements.

workedExamples: A tool used on suspect mold-affected material should not immediately return to unaffected harvest material without the controlled sanitation/segregation process.
commonMistakes: Treating harvest as lower-risk because cultivation is finished.
content.practicalApplication: Map a harvest workflow from plant to drying intake and identify contamination-control points, sanitation records and stop/escalation boundaries.
content.summary: Sanitary harvest handling protects product and traceability from the first cut onward.
